claim: Starch is the major nutritional component of staple crops.

claim: Starch is a feedstock for industry.
source: Starch, as the major nutritional component of our staple crops and a feedstock for industry, is a vital plant product.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about starch's industrial applications.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Starch is comprised of two α-polyglucan components: amylopectin and amylose.
source: Starch is comprised of two α-polyglucan components (here named glucans): large moderately-branched amylopectin molecules and interspersing small, near-linear amylose molecules (Manners, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Amylopectin molecules are large and moderately-branched.
source: Starch is comprised of two α-polyglucan components (here named glucans): large moderately-branched amylopectin molecules and interspersing small, near-linear amylose molecules (Manners, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Amylose molecules are small and near-linear.
source: Starch is comprised of two α-polyglucan components (here named glucans): large moderately-branched amylopectin molecules and interspersing small, near-linear amylose molecules (Manners, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Both amylopectin and amylose are built from chains of α-1,4 linked glucose units that are connected via α-1,6-linkages.
source: Both are built from chains of α-1,4 linked glucose units that are connected via α-1,6-linkages (branch points).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the chemical structure of starch components.

claim: In amylopectin, the branching pattern is non-random, giving rise to clusters of unbranched chain segments.
source: In amylopectin, the major and essential component, the branching pattern is non-random, giving rise to clusters of unbranched chain segments (Pérez and Bertoft, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Neighboring chains within amylopectin clusters form double helices that pack with distinct inter-helical spacing.
source: Neighboring chains within these clusters form double helices that pack with distinct inter-helical spacing.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of amylopectin structure.

claim: Crystalline lamellae in amylopectin alternate with amorphous lamellae containing the branch points.
source: The resulting crystalline lamellae, alternating with amorphous lamellae containing the branch points, stack with a periodicity of ~9–10.5 nm (Jenkins et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Crystalline and amorphous lamellae in amylopectin stack with a periodicity of ~9–10.5 nm.
source: The resulting crystalline lamellae, alternating with amorphous lamellae containing the branch points, stack with a periodicity of ~9–10.5 nm (Jenkins et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The unique semi-crystalline nature of amylopectin renders starch insoluble.
source: This unique semi-crystalline nature of amylopectin renders starch insoluble.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of amylopectin structure.

claim: Amylopectin biosynthesis involves four classes of starch synthases (SSs).
source: Amylopectin biosynthesis involves multiple enzyme activities, often composed of several isoforms with distinct specificities: four classes of starch synthases (SSs) elongate glucan chains using ADPglucose as glucosyl donor, creating α-1,4 glucose linkages
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the enzymes involved in amylopectin biosynthesis.

claim: Starch synthases elongate glucan chains using ADPglucose as glucosyl donor, creating α-1,4 glucose linkages.
source: four classes of starch synthases (SSs) elongate glucan chains using ADPglucose as glucosyl donor, creating α-1,4 glucose linkages
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of starch synthase function.

claim: Amylopectin biosynthesis involves two classes of branching enzymes (BEs).
source: two classes of branching enzymes (BEs) introduce branches in the form of α-1,6 linked chains
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the enzymes involved in amylopectin biosynthesis.

claim: Branching enzymes introduce branches in the form of α-1,6 linked chains.
source: two classes of branching enzymes (BEs) introduce branches in the form of α-1,6 linked chains
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of branching enzyme function.

claim: At least one isoamylase-type debranching enzyme hydrolyzes some branches, probably tailoring the glucan for crystallization.
source: and at least one isoamylase-type debranching enzyme hydrolyzes some branches again, probably tailoring the glucan for crystallization (Pfister and Zeeman, 2016; Tetlow and Emes, 2011; Zeeman et al., 2010; Jeon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Amylose is synthesized by a single class of granule-bound starch synthases.
source: In contrast, amylose is synthesized by a single class of granule-bound starch synthases (Denyer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: All starch synthases belong to the glycosyltransferase family 5 (GT5).
source: According to the classification of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZy; Lombard et al., 2014), all SSs belong to the glycosyltransferase family 5 (GT5)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Branching enzymes and isoamylases belong to distinct subfamilies of the glycoside hydrolase family 13 (GH13).
source: while BEs and isoamylases belong to distinct subfamilies of the glycoside hydrolase family 13 (GH13).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a classification of these enzymes.

claim: Starches from different plants vary in terms of amylose content, amylopectin structure and glucan modifications.
source: Starches from different plants vary in terms of amylose content, amylopectin structure and glucan modifications (e.g. level of phosphorylation) (Santelia and Zeeman, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Current starch variation cannot fully meet industrial needs, necessitating costly physicochemical modifications post-extraction.
source: However, to date, this variation cannot fully meet industrial needs, necessitating costly physicochemical modifications post-extraction to yield the desired properties (Tharanathan, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The starch-biosynthetic enzymes are highly conserved.
source: Although the starch-biosynthetic enzymes are highly conserved, we still do not have sufficient knowledge required for the rational modification of starch structure and properties in crops.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: There is insufficient knowledge required for the rational modification of starch structure and properties in crops.
source: Although the starch-biosynthetic enzymes are highly conserved, we still do not have sufficient knowledge required for the rational modification of starch structure and properties in crops.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a current limitation in the field.

claim: The difficulty in generating plant mutants hinders a systematic analysis in most species.
source: This deficiency has several roots; first, the difficulty in generating plant mutants hinders a systematic analysis in most species.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of plant-based research.

claim: Results obtained from comparable mutants in different plant systems are not always identical.
source: Second, the results obtained from comparable mutants in different plant systems are not always identical (e.g. due to variation in genetic, environmental and/or developmental backgrounds).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of plant-based research.

claim: Enzyme kinetics obtained from soluble substrates in vitro may not be representative of how an enzyme acts on a crystallizing surface in vivo.
source: Third, enzyme kinetics obtained from soluble substrates in vitro may not be representative of how an enzyme acts on a crystallizing surface in vivo (O'Neill and Field, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The glucans that make up starch are polydisperse, necessitating multiple biochemical and biophysical techniques for their structural characterization.
source: These problems are further compounded by the fact that the glucans that make up starch are polydisperse, necessitating multiple biochemical and biophysical techniques for their structural characterization.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a challenge in starch research.

claim: Progress in engineering new starches with enhanced functionalities in planta has been empirical and slow.
source: As a result, progress in engineering new starches with enhanced functionalities in planta has been empirical and slow, and the full potential of this important renewable resource has not been realized.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of current limitations.

claim: A model system in yeast was created that allows the expression of multiple starch-biosynthetic enzyme combinations in a targeted, controlled and fast manner.
source: Here we created a model system in yeast that allows the expression of multiple starch-biosynthetic enzyme combinations in a targeted, controlled and fast manner.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the main contribution of the study.

claim: The enzymes expressed in yeast are functional and capable of producing semi-crystalline starch-like granules in the right combinations.
source: Using a suite of molecular and biochemical analyses, we show that the enzymes are functional and, in the right combinations, capable of producing semi-crystalline starch-like granules.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: The yeast system is a highly tractable experimental system in which starch biosynthesis can be simulated.
source: This shows that our yeast system is a highly tractable experimental system in which starch biosynthesis can be simulated and the capacities of different interdependent enzymatic combinations can be evaluated, bringing us much closer to a holistic view of this critical process.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion about the utility of the system.

claim: The yeast expression platform employs haploid Saccharomyces cerevisiae CEN.PK113-11C.
source: Our yeast system employs an expression platform in haploid Saccharomyces cerevisiae CEN.PK113-11C, which had been developed for stable heterologous gene expression (Mikkelsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: Five genes involved in glycogen biosynthesis were purged from the yeast.
source: To eliminate interfering effects from the yeast's endogenous glycogen metabolic pathway, we purged it of the five genes involved in glycogen biosynthesis (two glycogenins, two glycogen synthases and glycogen branching enzyme)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: Two genes involved in glycogen degradation were purged from the yeast.
source: and two involved in glycogen degradation (glycogen debranching enzyme and α-glucan phosphorylase; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: All known amylopectin-biosynthetic genes from Arabidopsis thaliana were introduced into the yeast via stable integration.
source: We simultaneously introduced all known amylopectin-biosynthetic genes from Arabidopsis thaliana via stable integration of coding sequences driven by galactose-inducible promoters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: ISA1 and ISA2 together form the active heteromultimer named ISA.
source: ISA1 and ISA2 together form the active heteromultimer that here we name ISA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the isoamylase complex.

claim: BE1 is a third Arabidopsis gene annotated as branching enzyme.
source: Furthermore, we tested BE1 (At3g20440), a third Arabidopsis gene annotated as branching enzyme (Han et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: BE1 is distantly related to known branching enzymes.
source: This gene is distantly related to known branching enzymes, but studies to date have not revealed any starch-related function (Dumez et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Studies to date have not revealed any starch-related function for BE1.
source: This gene is distantly related to known branching enzymes, but studies to date have not revealed any starch-related function (Dumez et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Arabidopsis was chosen as the donor for amylopectin-biosynthetic genes because it has been intensively used for starch research.
source: Arabidopsis was chosen as the donor for amylopectin-biosynthetic genes because it has been intensively used for starch research, resulting in well-characterized mutants that enable us to make direct comparisons between yeast- and plant-derived glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as justification for the choice of organism.

claim: A non-regulated form of ADPglucose pyrophosphorylase from Escherichia coli (GlgC-TM) was introduced into the yeast.
source: In addition, we introduced a non-regulated form of ADPglucose pyrophosphorylase from Escherichia coli (GlgC-TM; Sakulsingharoj et al., 2004), as yeast glycogen biosynthesis is UDPglucose dependent, while the plant starch biosynthesis is ADPglucose dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Yeast glycogen biosynthesis is UDPglucose dependent.
source: as yeast glycogen biosynthesis is UDPglucose dependent, while the plant starch biosynthesis is ADPglucose dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as background information.

claim: Plant starch biosynthesis is ADPglucose dependent.
source: as yeast glycogen biosynthesis is UDPglucose dependent, while the plant starch biosynthesis is ADPglucose dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as background information.

claim: Each heterologously expressed enzyme was expressed and active in yeast.
source: Zymograms of soluble native protein extracts from yeast strains expressing ISA and single isoforms of SS and BE showed that each enzyme was expressed and active (SS1: lines 0 and 1; SS2: lines 2 and 3; SS3: line 5; SS4: line 7; BE2: line T; BE3: line S; ISA: all lines with uneven numbers; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by zymogram data in Figure 2A.

claim: The heterologously expressed enzymes migrated similarly to those in extracts of wild-type Arabidopsis plant controls.
source: The enzymes migrated similarly as in extracts of the wild-type (WT) Arabidopsis plant controls, even though we noted additional activity bands in some cases, possibly due to small alterations in post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 2A.

claim: Additional activity bands observed in some cases may be due to small alterations in post-translational modifications.
source: The enzymes migrated similarly as in extracts of the wild-type (WT) Arabidopsis plant controls, even though we noted additional activity bands in some cases, possibly due to small alterations in post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a possible explanation for observed differences.

claim: Protein activity varied in strength between some yeast lines.
source: Occasionally, we observed that protein activity varied in strength between the lines (e.g. SS2 activity between lines 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 2A.

claim: The enzyme's binding to insoluble glucans potentially affects its extractability as a soluble protein.
source: We reasoned that the enzyme's binding to insoluble glucans potentially accumulating in these lines may affect its extractability as a soluble protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for observed variation.

claim: Protein abundance detected in Western blots using total protein extracts was more uniform than in soluble extracts.
source: Indeed, protein abundance detected in Western blots using total protein extracts – where proteins in the insoluble fractions had been solubilized by boiling in SDS-containing buffer – was more uniform (Figure 2B), suggesting that expression levels between individual lines are in fact comparable.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression levels between individual yeast lines are comparable.
source: Indeed, protein abundance detected in Western blots using total protein extracts – where proteins in the insoluble fractions had been solubilized by boiling in SDS-containing buffer – was more uniform (Figure 2B), suggesting that expression levels between individual lines are in fact comparable.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from Western blot data.

claim: Plant BE2 or BE3 enabled substantial glucan production in yeast cells lacking their endogenous BE.
source: Either plant BE2 or BE3 enabled substantial glucan production in yeast cells lacking their endogenous BE (strains X and Y; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BE1 expression resulted in only low amounts of amylose-like glucans.
source: This was, however, not the case for strains expressing BE1. Here, only low amounts of amylose-like glucans could be detected (strains V and W), comparable to the strain lacking any branching enzyme (strain U; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: BE1 is not a starch branching enzyme.
source: This suggests that BE1 in fact is not a starch branching enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The presence of BE1 did not alter the glucans made by the other amylopectin biosynthetic enzymes.
source: Since the presence of BE1 also did not alter the glucans made by the other amylopectin biosynthetic enzymes, it was excluded from subsequent strain sets (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and associated text).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Every plant SS produced glucans when expressed as the sole synthase activity.
source: In contrast, every plant SS produced glucans when expressed as the sole synthase activity (lines 0, 2, 4 and 6; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of ISA in wild-type yeast suppressed the accumulation of glycogen.
source: Expression of ISA in wild-type yeast suppressed the accumulation of glycogen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Expression of ISA in E. coli reduced glycogen accumulation.
source: This result was consistent with that observed when expressing ISA in E. coli, where it also reduced glycogen accumulation (Sundberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Branch-point hydrolysis by ISA may have a degrading effect when provided with glycogen as a substrate.
source: Branch-point hydrolysis by ISA may have a degrading effect when it is provided with glycogen as a substrate rather than an amylopectin 'precursor'.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the observed effect.

claim: Amylopectin 'precursor' presumably crystallizes upon debranching, rendering it inaccessible to further modification.
source: The latter presumably crystallizes upon debranching, rendering it inaccessible to further modification (Sundberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A library of over 100 yeast lines was created.
source: Having established the functionality of the heterologous starch-biosynthetic enzymes, we created a library of over 100 yeast lines.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental approach.

claim: The library included 30 lines in the mutant background deficient in the endogenous glycogen-metabolic genes.
source: This collection included 30 lines in the mutant background deficient in the endogenous glycogen-metabolic genes (lines 0–29, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the library composition.

claim: In the 30 yeast lines, the complement of the four SS isoforms and ISA was systematically varied while keeping GlgC-TM, BE2 and BE3 constant.
source: In these lines, we systematically varied the complement of the four SS isoforms and ISA while keeping GlgC-TM, BE2 and BE3 constant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental design.

claim: No loss of heterologous genes could be detected by PCR in line 29 during strain maintenance and growth in liquid cultures.
source: No loss of heterologous genes could be detected by PCR in line 29 (carrying the highest number of modifications) during strain maintenance and growth in liquid cultures, indicating genetic stability (described in Materials and methods, not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as evidence of genetic stability.

claim: The engineered yeast lines stained in a variety of shades after iodine staining, suggesting they produced glucans with different structures.
source: The engineered yeast lines stained in a variety of shades, suggesting that they produced glucans with different structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 3A.

claim: Yeast strains expressing ISA tended to stain darker than their ISA-free counterparts.
source: Notably, yeast strains expressing ISA (lines with odd numbers; + ISA) tended to stain darker than their ISA-free counterparts (lines with even numbers; – ISA; placed above).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 3A.

claim: Most lines without ISA synthesized high amounts of soluble glucans, reaching around 10% of the wet weight.
source: Most lines without ISA synthesized high amounts of soluble glucans, which reached around 10% of the wet weight (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Light microscopy of yeast lines without ISA revealed fairly uniform iodine staining.
source: Light microscopy (LM) of these cells revealed fairly uniform iodine staining (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transmission electron micrographs from line 28 indicated numerous small particles reminiscent of glycogen.
source: Transmission electron micrographs (TEM) from line 28 indicated numerous small particles reminiscent of glycogen (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 3D.

claim: Cells expressing just SS1 as a synthase accumulated far fewer glucans than lines expressing the other SS isoforms.
source: Interestingly, cells expressing just SS1 as a synthase (line 0) accumulated far fewer glucans than lines expressing the other SS isoforms (lines 2, 4 and 6; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: In yeast lines still containing the endogenous glycogenins, all SS isoforms synthesized large amounts of glucan.
source: However, in yeast lines still containing the endogenous glycogenins, all SS isoforms synthesized large amounts of glucan (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; see figure legend for details).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SS1 is less efficient than the other SSs in utilizing available primers or in generating its own.
source: This suggests that, rather than having low activity, SS1 is less efficient than the other SSs in utilizing available primers or in generating its own.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Most lines expressing ISA produced water-insoluble glucans as well as soluble glucans.
source: Most lines expressing ISA produced water-insoluble glucans as well as soluble glucans (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lines expressing ISA accumulated linear malto-oligosaccharides, most likely representing chains liberated by ISA.
source: These lines also accumulated linear malto-oligosaccharides, most likely representing chains liberated by ISA (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The presence of insoluble glucans was typically associated with discrete, patchy staining of cells in light microscopy.
source: The presence of insoluble glucans was typically associated with discrete, patchy staining of cells in LM (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TEMs from line 29 showed solid continuous glucan particles which often occupied a significant fraction of the yeast cell volume.
source: TEMs from line 29 showed solid continuous glucan particles which often occupied a significant fraction of the yeast cell volume in addition to small, presumably soluble glucan particles (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 3D.

claim: Lines which expressed ISA but neither SS3 nor SS4 had very low glucan levels when grown in liquid culture.
source: Interestingly, the lines which expressed ISA but neither SS3 nor SS4 (lines 1, 3 and 9) had very low glucan levels when grown in liquid culture (lines 1 and 3, Figure 3B; line 9, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; see also lines F, G, J and K, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: Hydrolysis by ISA may limit glucan accumulation under some conditions.
source: This again indicates that hydrolysis by ISA may limit glucan accumulation under some conditions (as described above).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: ISA enabled the synthesis of insoluble glucans.
source: As mentioned, ISA enabled the synthesis of insoluble glucans (also see Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in figures.

claim: SS isoforms have a clear effect on the synthesis of insoluble glucans when ISA was present.
source: Moreover, we observed a clear effect of SS isoforms on the synthesis of insoluble glucans when ISA was present.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: SS4 consistently promoted the synthesis of insoluble glucans, both in absolute and relative terms.
source: Comparing the percentages of insoluble glucans of strains with and without SS4 (e.g., strain 25 vs. strain 11) revealed that SS4 consistently promoted the synthesis of insoluble glucans, both in absolute and relative terms (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: SS1 activity rendered the glucans less insoluble and consistently promoted the synthesis of soluble glucans.
source: In contrast, SS1 activity rendered the glucans less insoluble and consistently promoted the synthesis of soluble glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: The presence of SS2 had variable effects, but significantly increased the percentage of insoluble glucans in the absence of SS4.
source: The presence of SS2 had variable effects, but significantly increased the percentage of insoluble glucans in the absence of SS4 (line 21 vs. 11: + 46%, line 15 vs. line 5: + 30%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: The increase in the proportion of insoluble glucans caused by SS4 was strongest in the lines without SS2.
source: Reciprocally, the increase in the proportion of insoluble glucans caused by SS4 was strongest in the lines without SS2 (line 25 vs. 11: + 108%; line 19 vs. 5: + 95%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Strain I and strain M, containing BE3 as sole BE and either SS2 or SS3, contained up to 19% of their glucans in an insoluble form.
source: Strain I and strain M, containing BE3 as sole BE and either SS2 or SS3, respectively, contained up to 19% of their glucans in an insoluble form (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The equivalent strains with both BEs contained only soluble glucans.
source: The equivalent strains with both BEs contained only soluble glucans (strains 2 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison.

claim: When together with SS3 and ISA, having BE3 alone promoted insoluble glucan formation.
source: An effect of BE on the partitioning between soluble and insoluble glucans could also be observed when ISA was present: When together with SS3 and ISA, having BE3 alone promoted insoluble glucan formation (compare strain O vs. 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: When together with SS4 and ISA, having BE3 alone reduced both the total glucan content and the percentage that was insoluble.
source: In contrast, when together with SS4 and ISA, having BE3 alone reduced both the total glucan content and the percentage that was insoluble.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Having BE3 alone rather than both BEs was accompanied by a shift towards longer wavelengths of maximum absorption after iodine staining.
source: In all instances, however, having BE3 alone rather than both BEs, was accompanied by a shift towards longer wavelengths of maximum absorption [λmax] after iodine staining.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Each enzyme activity influences insoluble glucan formation in a distinct manner.
source: Together, these data show that each enzyme activity influences insoluble glucan formation in a distinct manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: There is a complex functional interplay between both enzyme classes and isoenzymes of each class that are collectively responsible for starch synthesis.
source: They also highlight the complex functional interplay between both enzyme classes and isoenzymes of each class that are collectively responsible for starch synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: SS classes have distinct preferences in terms of glucan chain elongation.
source: Studies of plant mutants and of individual enzymes in in-vitro have suggested that SS classes have distinct preferences in terms of glucan chain elon gation (Zeeman et al., 2010; Tetlow and Emes, 2011; Pfister and Zeeman, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The presence of SS1 increased the relative abundance of shorter chains (DP = 6–10) at the expense of intermediate-length ones (DP = 11–25).
source: In all instances, the presence of SS1 increased the relative abundance of shorter chains (degree of polymerization or DP = 6–10) at the expense of intermediate-length ones (DP = 11–25) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The effect of SS1 on chain length distribution is in accordance with that from Arabidopsis and cereal mutants.
source: This result is in accordance with that from Arabidopsis (Figure 5B; Delvallé et al., 2005; Szydlowski et al., 2011) and cereal mutants (Fujita et al., 2006; McMaugh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and data in Figure 5B.

claim: The presence of SS2 had a consistent effect on the CLDs of yeast-derived glucans, increasing the relative abundance of intermediate-length chains.
source: Similarly, the presence of SS2 had a consistent effect on the CLDs of yeast-derived glucans, increasing the relative abundance of intermediate-length chains (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: The alterations in chain length distribution by SS2 were consistent with previous data of ss2 mutants from Arabidopsis and other species.
source: Again, these alterations were consistent with previous data of ss2 mutants from Arabidopsis and other species (Zhang et al., 2008; Edwards et al., 1999; Craig et al., 1998; Morell et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The magnitudes of SS1 and SS2 isoform-specific CLD alterations were smaller among the yeast glucans than among the plant glucans.
source: The magnitudes of these isoform-specific CLD alterations were smaller among the yeast glucans than among the plant glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between yeast and plant data.

claim: The smaller magnitude of CLD alterations in yeast is probably due to the overall relative increase in longer chains in the yeast glucans compared to Arabidopsis starch.
source: This is probably due to the overall relative increase in longer chains in the yeast glucans compared to Arabidopsis starch (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the observed difference.

claim: SS3 and SS4 did not influence the lengths of short and intermediate chains in a distinct manner.
source: SS3 and SS4 did not influence the lengths of short and intermediate chains in a distinct manner (not shown), which is in-line with reports from Arabidopsis mutants (Zhang et al., 2005; Roldán et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The tendency of SS3 to increase the abundance of intermediate-length chains in the absence of SS2 was apparent in yeast.
source: However, the tendency of SS3 to increase the abundance of intermediate-length chains in the absence of SS2 (Zhang et al., 2008) was also apparent in yeast (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and data in Figure 5D.

claim: The insoluble glucans from line 29 were laid down as distinct spherical particles that were several micrometers in diameter.
source: The insoluble glucans were laid down as distinct spherical particles that were several micrometers in diameter, as determined by scanning electron microscopy (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 6A.

claim: The size of the insoluble glucan particles from line 29 was within the range observed for plant starch granules.
source: The size of these particles was within the range observed for plant starch granules (Pérez and Bertoft, 2010), including Arabidopsis leaf starch (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and comparison in Figure 6A.

claim: Similar particles could be purified from other yeast strains producing insoluble glucans.
source: Similar, albeit not identical, particles could be purified from other yeast strains producing insoluble glucans, but not from those lacking measurable insoluble glucans (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6A.

claim: Cells of line 29 contained regions of high density (putatively insoluble glucans) as well as regions of intermediate density (probably reflecting soluble glucans).
source: Cells of line 29 contained regions of a high density - putatively insoluble glucans - as well as regions of intermediate density, probably reflecting soluble glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 6B.

claim: The high-density regions in line 29 cells had a density identical to that of Arabidopsis amylopectin.
source: Remarkably, the high-density regions had a density identical to that of Arabidopsis amylopectin, pointing towards a comparable internal organization of the glucans (mean electron density [± S.D., n = 6] from line 29 = 0.44 ± 0.01 e−Å−3, corresponding to a mass density of 1.36 ± 0.04 g mL−1; Arabidopsis amylopectin density = 0.441 ± 0.004 e- Å−3, corresponding to 1.36 ± 0.01 g mL−1; see Materials and methods for details) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with quantitative data and can be observed in Figure 6B.

claim: The absorption characteristics of the insoluble glucans after iodine complexion from line 29 were almost identical to those of amylopectins from wild-type and gbss mutant plants (λmax ~548 nm).
source: Further, the absorption characteristics of the insoluble glucans after iodine complexion from line 29 were almost identical to those of amylopectins from wild-type and gbss mutant plants (λmax after iodine-complexion of ~548 nm; Figure 6C; [Zeeman et al., 2002b]).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and data in Figure 6C.

claim: The insoluble glucans from line 29 were distinct from highly-branched, soluble glycogen from wild-type yeast (λmax 445 nm).
source: In addition, they were distinct from that of highly-branched, soluble glycogen from wild-type yeast (λmax445 nm)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 6C.

claim: The insoluble glucans from line 29 were distinct from soluble glucans from line 28 (λmax 505 nm).
source: from that of soluble glucans from the corresponding line without ISA (line 28, λmax505 nm)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 6C.

claim: The insoluble glucans from line 29 were distinct from linear glucans such as potato amylose (λmax 634 nm).
source: and from that of linear glucans such as potato amylose (λmax634 nm).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed in Figure 6C.

claim: The similarity in absorption spectra indicates that the insoluble glucans from line 29 form comparable secondary structures to those in plant amylopectin, i.e. double helices between adjacent chains.
source: The similarity in absorption spectra indicates that the insoluble glucans from line 29 form comparable secondary structures to those in plant amylopectin, i.e. double helices between adjacent chains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the spectroscopic data.

claim: The iodine absorption spectra of insoluble glucans from yeast strains expressing only subsets of SSs were dissimilar to that from line 29.
source: Notably, also the iodine absorption spectra of insoluble glucans from yeast strains expressing only subsets of SSs (e.g. SS3, line 5, or SS4, line 7, or SS1, SS2 and SS3, line 21) were dissimilar to that from line 29, re-affirming the influence of SSs on glucan structure (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Wide-angle X-ray scattering of purified and dried glucans from line 29 resulted in a diffraction pattern typical of many starches, indicative of a B-type allomorph.
source: Wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) of purified and dried glucans resulted in a diffraction pattern typical of many starches, where glucan chains form double helices that align with an inter-helical spacing of ~1.6 nm, indicative of a B-type allomorph (Kong et al., 2014; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and data in Figure 6D.

claim: Glucan chains in the insoluble glucans from line 29 form double helices that align with an inter-helical spacing of ~1.6 nm.
source: Wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) of purified and dried glucans resulted in a diffraction pattern typical of many starches, where glucan chains form double helices that align with an inter-helical spacing of ~1.6 nm, indicative of a B-type allomorph (Kong et al., 2014; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and data in Figure 6D.

claim: Small-angle X-ray scattering indicated that the helices in line 29 glucans were stacked in a weakly ordered lamellar structure with a periodicity of 13.6 nm.
source: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) indicated that the helices were stacked in a weakly ordered lamellar structure with a periodicity of 13.6 nm (Figure 6E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: The lamellar periodicity in line 29 glucans (13.6 nm) is slightly longer than typically reported for plant starches.
source: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) indicated that the helices were stacked in a weakly ordered lamellar structure with a periodicity of 13.6 nm (Figure 6E), slightly longer than typically reported for plant starches (Pérez and Bertoft, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and data in Figure 6E.

claim: Arabidopsis starch had a ~10.5 nm lamellar periodicity.
source: Here, Arabidopsis starch had a ~10.5 nm periodicity (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The insoluble glucans from line 29 had relatively more long chains (DP > 18) than wild-type Arabidopsis amylopectin.
source: Chain-length distribution (CLD) analyses revealed that the insoluble glucans had relatively more long chains (DP > 18) than wild-type Arabidopsis amylopectin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from CLD analysis.

claim: The key characteristics of amylopectin were preserved in line 29 glucans as they grouped in sub-populations of chains with DPs of 6–8, 9–18 and >18.
source: Nevertheless, the key characteristics of amylopectin were preserved as they grouped in sub-populations of chains with DPs of 6–8, 9–18 and >18 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: The insoluble glucans from line 29 form granular particles which display the typical internal organization of semi-crystalline plant starch.
source: Collectively, these analyses show that the insoluble glucans from line 29 form granular particles which display the typical internal organization of semi-crystalline plant starch.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary conclusion from multiple analyses.

claim: This study represents the first example of where insoluble, starch-like granules have been produced in a non-plant system.
source: To our knowledge, this study represents the first example of where insoluble, starch-like granules have been produced in a non-plant system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: This study provides direct evidence that SSs, BEs and ISA are all key enzymatic components for starch granule formation.
source: It provides direct evidence that SSs, BEs and ISA are all key enzymatic components for starch granule formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The heterologously expressed enzymes retain their specificities in yeast.
source: We furthermore show that the heterologously expressed enzymes retain their specificities in yeast
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The yeast system can be used as an advanced tool for studying the overall process of starch biosynthesis in unprecedented speed and depth.
source: and propose that this system can be used as an advanced tool for studying the overall process of starch biosynthesis in unprecedented speed and depth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal for future applications.

claim: A major obstacle associated with any plant-related approach is the presence of additional starch-active enzymes, some of which may not even be known.
source: A major obstacle associated with any plant-related approach is the presence of additional starch-active enzymes, some of which may not even be known.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of plant-based research.

claim: In Arabidopsis chloroplasts, there is a plethora of starch-catabolising enzymes.
source: In Arabidopsis chloroplasts, where starch is made and degraded during a single diurnal cycle, there is a plethora of starch-catabolising enzymes: the two additional debranching enzymes ISA3 (At4g09020) and limit-dextrinase (At5g04360), at least two active β-amylases (BAM1 [At3g23920] and BAM3 [At4g17090]), the α-amylase AMY3 (At1g69830), the disproportionating enzyme DPE1 (At5g64860) and the α-glucan phosphorylase PHS1 (At3g29320) (Zeeman et al., 2004, 2007; Delatte et al., 2006; Fulton et al., 2008; Seung et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Starch synthesis and degradation are regarded as separate processes in wild-type plants.
source: In general, starch synthesis and degradation are regarded as separate processes in wild-type plants.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as general knowledge.

claim: The rapid crystallization of correctly synthesized amylopectin may protect it from further modification by enzymes of starch degradation.
source: It is possible that the rapid crystallization of correctly synthesized amylopectin protects it from further modification by enzymes of starch degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: In Arabidopsis mutants deficient in multiple starch-biosynthetic enzymes, glucan synthesis and accumulation have been repeatedly shown to be influenced by degrading enzymes.
source: However, in Arabidopsis mutants deficient in multiple starch-biosynthetic enzymes, glucan synthesis and accumulation have been repeatedly shown to be influenced by degrading enzymes, for example in the isa1isa2 (Delatte et al., 2005), the be2be3 (Dumez et al., 2006), the isa1isa2isa3lda (Streb et al., 2008-), the ss2ss3 (Pfister et al., 2014) and the ss3ss4 mutant (Seung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: It has been very difficult to reliably ascribe the glucans produced in a plant's cell to the actions of a distinct enzymatic set.
source: Consequently, it has been very difficult to reliably ascribe the glucans produced in a plant's cell to the actions of a distinct enzymatic set.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a consequence of the complexity of plant systems.

claim: The approach used in this study to deduce the essential components for starch biosynthesis is more direct than plant-based approaches.
source: The approach we used here to deduce the essential components for starch biosynthesis is more direct.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison with plant-based approaches.

claim: Plant genes have been expressed in yeast or E. coli before.
source: Although plant genes have been expressed in yeast or E. coli before (Guan et al., 1995; Guan and Keeling, 1998; Seo et al., 2002), our study is unique in several ways.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The yeast used in this study is purged of its endogenous glycogen-metabolic pathway.
source: The yeast is purged of its endogenous glycogen-metabolic pathway and the introduced genes can be induced together.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a unique feature of the study.

claim: The introduced genes in the yeast system can be induced together.
source: The yeast is purged of its endogenous glycogen-metabolic pathway and the introduced genes can be induced together.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a unique feature of the study.

claim: The yeast system allows the study of starch biosynthesis independently of interfering background effects from the yeast itself or from the plant's degradative enzymes.
source: These factors allow us to study starch biosynthesis independently of interfering background effects from the yeast itself, or from the plant's degradative enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of the system.

claim: The systematic variation in enzyme combinations enables the contribution of each enzyme and capacities of different enzymatic sets to be analyzed in ways that were previously not possible.
source: This enables the contribution of each enzyme and capacities of different enzymatic sets to be analyzed in ways that were previously not possible.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of the systematic approach.

claim: Debranching by ISA is the major driving force for the formation of insoluble glucans.
source: Our work confirms that debranching by ISA is the major driving force for the formation of insoluble glucans: In most (but not all) cases, insoluble glucans were only obtained when ISA was present (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study, supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The promotion of insoluble glucans by ISA is in-line with plant mutants lacking this enzyme, which typically accumulate water-soluble polysaccharides, so-called phytoglycogen.
source: The promotion of insoluble glucans by ISA is in-line with plant mutants lacking this enzyme, which typically accumulate water-soluble polysaccharides, so-called phytoglycogen (Nakamura et al., 1996; Mouille et al., 1996; Zeeman et al., 1998; Dinges et al., 2001; Burton et al., 2002; Bustos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: ISA selectively hydrolyzes excessive or misplaced branches that would otherwise interfere with the formation of double helices.
source: Presumably, ISA selectively hydrolyzes excessive or misplaced branches that would otherwise interfere with the formation of double helices (Myers et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A pool of linear malto-oligosaccharides could be detected in strains where ISA promoted insoluble glucan formation.
source: Consistent with this, we could detect a pool of linear malto-oligosaccharides in strains where ISA promoted insoluble glucan formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In wild-type plants, malto-oligosaccharides are probably rapidly metabolized and therefore not detectable.
source: In wild-type plants, such a malto-oligosaccharide pool is probably rapidly metabolized and therefore not detectable (Streb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: When ISA was present, SS1 always decreased the production of insoluble glucans.
source: In the present study, we also dissected the contribution of SSs and BEs to insoluble glucan formation. When ISA was present, SS1 always decreased the production of insoluble glucans (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The decreased crystallinity of glucans in the presence of SS1 probably stems from the increased abundance of glucan chains of DP 6–10.
source: The decreased crystallinity of glucans in the presence of SS1 probably stems from the increased abundance of glucan chains of DP 6–10 (Figure 5B) that are too short to efficiently contribute to the formation of higher-order structures underlying starch crystallinity (Pfannemüller, 1987; Gidley and Bulpin, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations and data in Figure 5B.

claim: Glucan chains of DP 6–10 are too short to efficiently contribute to the formation of higher-order structures underlying starch crystallinity.
source: The decreased crystallinity of glucans in the presence of SS1 probably stems from the increased abundance of glucan chains of DP 6–10 (Figure 5B) that are too short to efficiently contribute to the formation of higher-order structures underlying starch crystallinity (Pfannemüller, 1987; Gidley and Bulpin, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: A comparable effect of SS1 has been described in Arabidopsis, where the lack of SS1 in the isa mutant background restored granule formation in the mesophyll cells.
source: We have recently described a comparable effect of SS1 in Arabidopsis, where the lack of SS1 in the isa mutant background restored granule formation in the mesophyll cells (Pfister et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: SS4 enhanced the production of insoluble glucans.
source: In contrast, SS4 enhanced the production of insoluble glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a finding from the study.

claim: The effect of SS4 on insoluble glucan production cannot be traced back to distinct structural modifications.
source: This effect cannot be traced back to distinct structural modifications – no consistent alterations in glucan structure by SS4 were observed in our comparisons or in studies of Arabidopsis ss4 mutants (data not shown; Roldán et al., 2007; Szydlowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The methods currently available for the analysis of starch structure give an incomplete picture.
source: One has to bear in mind, though, that the methods currently available for the analysis of starch structure give an incomplete picture, and structural features introduced by SS4 may not have been revealed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a caveat about current analytical methods.

claim: Structural features introduced by SS4 may not have been revealed by current analytical methods.
source: One has to bear in mind, though, that the methods currently available for the analysis of starch structure give an incomplete picture, and structural features introduced by SS4 may not have been revealed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possibility.

claim: Uniform effects upon the expression of SS2 and SS3 were not observed.
source: We did not observe uniform effects upon the expression of SS2 and SS3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: SS2 specifically elongates chains from around DP 8 to around DP 13.
source: For SS2, this was surprising; it has been shown that SS2 specifically elongates chains from around DP 8 to around DP 13 and suggested that this promotes the formation of higher-order structures (Nakamura et al., 2005; Fujita et al., 2012; Pfister et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: SS2 chain elongation promotes the formation of higher-order structures.
source: For SS2, this was surprising; it has been shown that SS2 specifically elongates chains from around DP 8 to around DP 13 and suggested that this promotes the formation of higher-order structures (Nakamura et al., 2005; Fujita et al., 2012; Pfister et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Mutation of SS2 in Arabidopsis results in small amounts of phytoglycogen.
source: Indeed, mutation of SS2 in Arabidopsis results in small amounts of phytoglycogen and enhances the accumulation of phytoglycogen in isa mutants of both rice and Arabidopsis (Fujita et al., 2012; Pfister et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Mutation of SS2 enhances the accumulation of phytoglycogen in isa mutants of both rice and Arabidopsis.
source: Indeed, mutation of SS2 in Arabidopsis results in small amounts of phytoglycogen and enhances the accumulation of phytoglycogen in isa mutants of both rice and Arabidopsis (Fujita et al., 2012; Pfister et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The alterations in glucan structure introduced by SS2 are preserved in the yeast system.
source: Although the alterations in glucan structure introduced by SS2 are preserved in the yeast system (Figure 5C), SS2 promoted the synthesis of insoluble glucans only when SS4 was absent (Figure 4B, comparisons in bold).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: SS2 promoted the synthesis of insoluble glucans only when SS4 was absent.
source: Although the alterations in glucan structure introduced by SS2 are preserved in the yeast system (Figure 5C), SS2 promoted the synthesis of insoluble glucans only when SS4 was absent (Figure 4B, comparisons in bold).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The strong effect of SS4 in promoting insoluble glucan formation may mask the effect of SS2 in yeast.
source: It is possible that the strong effect of SS4 in promoting insoluble glucan formation masks this effect of SS2 in yeast, potentially due to differences in relative expression levels compared to Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation.

claim: In some lines expressing only BE3 as a branching enzyme, insoluble glucans were obtained despite the absence of any debranching activity.
source: Our data also add new insights into how branching level influences the synthesis of insoluble glucans: In some lines expressing only BE3 as a branching enzyme, insoluble glucans were obtained despite the absence of any debranching activity (Figure 4C), confirming that the latter is not an absolute requirement for the insoluble-glucan production (Streb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Debranching activity is not an absolute requirement for insoluble-glucan production.
source: In some lines expressing only BE3 as a branching enzyme, insoluble glucans were obtained despite the absence of any debranching activity (Figure 4C), confirming that the latter is not an absolute requirement for the insoluble-glucan production (Streb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: BE2 and BE3 are closely related class II BEs and largely redundant in Arabidopsis.
source: BE2 and BE3 are closely related class II BEs and largely redundant in Arabidopsis (Dumez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The impact of having only BE3 is probably due to overall branching activity rather than to a difference in specificity.
source: Therefore, the impact of having only BE3 is probably due to overall branching activity rather than to a difference in specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: In combination with some, but not all SS, low BE activity resulted in formation of insoluble glucans.
source: It is striking that in combination with some, but not all SS this low BE activity resulted in formation of insoluble glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation from the data.

claim: In all cases where BE3 alone was present, the λmax of the iodine-stained glucans increased, suggesting that the structure was altered in a similar way.
source: This was despite the fact that in all cases the λmax of the iodine-stained glucans increased, suggesting that the structure was altered in a similar way, i.e. more chains long enough to form single or double helices were present.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation from the data.

claim: Secondary structures (single or double helices) are not sufficient for insoluble glucan formation.
source: Clearly, such secondary structures are not sufficient for insoluble glucan formation, presumably because they need also to align in parallel to form a semi-crystalline matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Helices need to align in parallel to form a semi-crystalline matrix for insoluble glucan formation.
source: Clearly, such secondary structures are not sufficient for insoluble glucan formation, presumably because they need also to align in parallel to form a semi-crystalline matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: Glycogen biosynthesis in yeast and animals begins with the self-glycosylation of glycogenins on tyrosine residues.
source: Glycogen biosynthesis in yeast and animals begins with the self-glycosylation of glycogenins on tyrosine residues, yielding short glucan chains that are then elongated by glycogen synthases (Rodriguez and Whelan, 1985; Lomako et al., 1988; Pitcher et al., 1988; Cheng et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The mechanism of starch initiation is not known.
source: In contrast, the mechanism of starch initiation is not known.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a gap in knowledge.

claim: In Arabidopsis, genetic evidence suggests a specialized role for SS4 in starch initiation since ss4 mutants display a strong reduction in starch granule number.
source: In Arabidopsis, genetic evidence suggests a specialized role for SS4 in this process since ss4 mutants display a strong reduction in starch granule number (Roldán et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: ss3 mutants have normal number of starch granules.
source: Although ss3 mutants have normal number of starch granules (Seung et al., 2016), further loss of SS3 from the ss4 mutant background resulted in a nearly complete failure of glucan synthesis (Szydlowski et al., 2009), indicating that SS3 becomes indispensable for glucan priming when SS4 is absent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Further loss of SS3 from the ss4 mutant background resulted in a nearly complete failure of glucan synthesis.
source: Although ss3 mutants have normal number of starch granules (Seung et al., 2016), further loss of SS3 from the ss4 mutant background resulted in a nearly complete failure of glucan synthesis (Szydlowski et al., 2009), indicating that SS3 becomes indispensable for glucan priming when SS4 is absent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: SS3 becomes indispensable for glucan priming when SS4 is absent.
source: Although ss3 mutants have normal number of starch granules (Seung et al., 2016), further loss of SS3 from the ss4 mutant background resulted in a nearly complete failure of glucan synthesis (Szydlowski et al., 2009), indicating that SS3 becomes indispensable for glucan priming when SS4 is absent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: It is unclear what primes glucan synthesis in the yeast strains.
source: In our yeast strains, it is unclear what primes glucan synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an open question.

claim: SS1 has limited capacity to initiate glucan synthesis, but can use primers provided by glycogenins.
source: This phenotype is reminiscent of the yeast glycogenin mutant (glg1glg2) which synthesizes only little glycogen overall but accumulates it in single colonies, presumably due to stochastic initiation events (Torija et al., 2005). This suggests that, similar to yeast glycogen synthases, SS1 has limited capacity to initiate glucan synthesis, but can use primers provided by glycogenins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: SS2 also synthesized slightly fewer glucans when glycogenins were absent.
source: It is worth noting that SS2 also synthesized slightly fewer glucans when glycogenins were absent (strain H vs. I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Degradation influences glucan initiation.
source: Our study also suggests that degradation influences glucan initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The absence of malto-oligosaccharides in lines with only SS1 and/or SS2 and ISA argues against excessive debranching by ISA.
source: However, the absence of malto-oligosaccharides - the expected products of ISA action - in these lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) argues against such a scenario.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Degradation by ISA may happen at a very early time point and could impair the glucan synthesis altogether by limiting the availability of primers.
source: Rather, the degradation may happen at a very early time point and could impair the glucan synthesis altogether by limiting the availability of primers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an alternative explanation.

claim: Arabidopsis ss3ss4 mutants are virtually glucan-free due to an apparent failure in the priming of glucan synthesis.
source: This observation is particularly interesting since Arabidopsis ss3ss4 mutants are virtually glucan-free due to an apparent failure in the priming of glucan synthesis (Szydlowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The additional knock-out of the α-amylase AMY3 in ss4 Arabidopsis mutants increases granule number and overall starch content.
source: Indeed, it was recently shown that the additional knock-out of the α-amylase AMY3 in ss4 Arabidopsis mutants increases granule number and overall starch content, and loss of AMY3 in ss3ss4 Arabidopsis mutants (amy3ss3ss4 mutants) even restored some granule formation (Seung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Loss of AMY3 in ss3ss4 Arabidopsis mutants restored some granule formation.
source: Indeed, it was recently shown that the additional knock-out of the α-amylase AMY3 in ss4 Arabidopsis mutants increases granule number and overall starch content, and loss of AMY3 in ss3ss4 Arabidopsis mutants (amy3ss3ss4 mutants) even restored some granule formation (Seung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: At least part of the priming function of SS4 lies in the protection of primers from premature degradation.
source: These phenotypes were interpreted to mean that at least part of the priming function of SS4 lies in the protection of primers from premature degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of published results.

claim: ISA may diminish primers, which could explain why glucan accumulation in amy3ss3ss4 mutants is only partially restored.
source: Our observation that ISA may also diminish primers could explain why glucan accumulation in amy3ss3ss4 mutants is only partially restored.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation connecting the yeast and plant data.

claim: ISA has been implicated as a negative regulator of granule initiation before, since the remaining starch of isa mutants is typically deposited as numerous small granules.
source: Notably, ISA has been implicated as a negative regulator of granule initiation before, since the remaining starch of isa mutants is typically deposited as numerous small granules (Burton et al., 2002; Bustos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The granules made in yeast by the Arabidopsis enzymes are not identical to those made by Arabidopsis itself.
source: It is interesting - but perhaps not surprising - that the granules made in yeast by the Arabidopsis enzymes are not identical to those made by Arabidopsis itself.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: Long chains (DP > 18) were overrepresented in the yeast glucans, in particular when ISA was present.
source: For instance, long chains (DP > 18) were overrepresented in the yeast glucans, in particular when ISA was present (Figure 5A and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: In plant amylopectin, the group of chains with DP < 25 is believed to make up a single 9- to 10.5-nm-repeat.
source: In plant amylopectin, the group of chains with DP < 25 is believed to make up a single 9- to 10.5-nm-repeat, being part of the double helices that underlie starch crystallinity (so-called A and B1 chains; Hizukuri [1986]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The relative abundance of long chains in yeast glucans may explain the increased width of the lamellar repeat observed (13.6 nm).
source: Since the length of these chains probably defines the width of the lamellar repeat, the relative abundance of long chains in yeast glucans may explain the increased width of the repeat we observed (13.6 nm in the insoluble glucans from line 29; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The molecular factors determining the width of the lamellar repeat are not known.
source: The molecular factors determining the width of the lamellar repeat are not known, but were suggested to involve the specific placement of branches by BEs (Nakamura, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A wild-type lamellar repeat distance was not obtained despite having expressed both known starch BEs from Arabidopsis.
source: Nonetheless, we did not obtain a wild-type repeat distance, despite having expressed both known starch BEs from Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: Most plants contain an additional BE of class I, which displays distinct specificities when assessed in vitro.
source: Most plants contain an additional BE of class I, which displays distinct specificities when assessed in vitro (Rydberg et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 2010; Sawada et al., 2014), but the Arabidopsis' genome does not encode such a BE (Dumez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The Arabidopsis genome does not encode a class I BE.
source: Most plants contain an additional BE of class I, which displays distinct specificities when assessed in vitro (Rydberg et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 2010; Sawada et al., 2014), but the Arabidopsis' genome does not encode such a BE (Dumez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The data do not support the idea that the gene annotated as BE1 in Arabidopsis represents a third BE activity.
source: In-line with earlier reports (Dumez et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2010), our data also do not support the idea that the gene annotated as BE1 in Arabidopsis represents a third BE activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations and data.

claim: Differences in the relative amounts of each enzyme between the yeast lines and Arabidopsis are likely.
source: While we believe that we have expressed the right enzyme combinations, differences in the relative amounts of each enzyme between the yeast lines and Arabidopsis are likely.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a caveat.

claim: BE activities according to zymograms appear comparable in yeast and in Arabidopsis leaves.
source: Indeed, although the BE activities according to our zymograms appear comparable in yeast and in Arabidopsis leaves, some SS activities differ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and can be observed in Figure 2A.

claim: SS3 activity was elevated in yeast compared with Arabidopsis.
source: In particular, SS3 activity was elevated in yeast compared with Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: SS4 was proposed to contribute only little to chain elongation in Arabidopsis.
source: The same may be true for SS4, which was proposed to contribute only little to chain elongation in Arabidopsis (Szydlowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The repression or mutation of class II BEs causes the so-called amylose-extender phenotype, where amylopectin is characterized by longer chains.
source: It is interesting to note that the repression or mutation of class II BEs causes the so-called amylose-extender phenotype, where amylopectin is characterized by longer chains (Boyer et al., 1980; Hedman and Boyer, 1982; Mizuno et al., 1993; Sestili et al., 2010; Regina et al., 2010; Klucinec and Thompson, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: In barley, the amylose-extender phenotype was shown to be accompanied by a longer lamellar repeat (12.5 nm instead of 10.4 nm).
source: In barley, this was shown to be accompanied by a longer lamellar repeat (12.5 nm instead of 10.4 nm; Regina et al., [2012]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: It is unclear whether the amylose-extender phenotype reflects a limitation of overall BE activity or the specificity of the remaining class I BE, or both.
source: However, it is unclear whether this phenotype reflects a limitation of overall BE activity (creating an imbalance with chain elongation) or the specificity of the remaining class I BE, or both.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an open question.

claim: An impact on amylopectin structure either by BE specificity or by the amount of BE activity relative to the other starch-biosynthetic enzymes was shown directly in a molecular genetic approach.
source: In a recent molecular genetic approach, an impact on amylopectin structure either by BE specificity or by the amount of BE activity relative to the other starch-biosynthetic enzymes was shown directly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a reference to recent work.

claim: Lu et al., (2015) complemented the be2be3 Arabidopsis mutant with class I or class II BEs.
source: Lu et al., (2015) complemented the be2be3 Arabidopsis mutant with class I or class II BEs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of published work.

claim: When either BE activity was limiting, it resulted in decreased amounts of starch and amylopectin with a higher proportion of chains of DP > 18.
source: Analysis of different transgenic lines established that when either BE activity was limiting, it resulted in decreased amounts of starch and amylopectin with a higher proportion of chains of DP > 18, compared with when the same BE was expressed at higher levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a finding from published work.

claim: Every yeast strain accumulated substantial amounts of soluble glucans.
source: Another difference between the glucans made in yeast and in plant cells concerns the presence of soluble polysaccharides: while virtually all plant glucans are normally laid down as insoluble starch granules, every yeast strain accumulated also substantial amounts of soluble glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: Virtually all plant glucans are normally laid down as insoluble starch granules.
source: Another difference between the glucans made in yeast and in plant cells concerns the presence of soluble polysaccharides: while virtually all plant glucans are normally laid down as insoluble starch granules, every yeast strain accumulated also substantial amounts of soluble glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as background information.

claim: The percentages of insoluble glucans from total glucans varied depending on the complement of enzymes present.
source: The percentages of insoluble glucans from total glucans varied depending on the complement of enzymes present (as discussed above).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: The percentage of insoluble glucans did not exceed ~70% in the best cases.
source: Still, it did not exceed ~70% in the best cases (strains O and N, Figure 4C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in figures.

claim: The percentage of insoluble glucans ranged between 17 and 58% when ISA and both BEs were present.
source: and ranged between 17 and 58% when ISA and both BEs were present (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The incomplete formation of insoluble glucans in yeast could be a matter of enzyme balance.
source: This incomplete formation of insoluble glucans in yeast can have several reasons. First, it could again be a matter of enzyme balance, although we do not know of a comparable instance from plants here.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation.

claim: The efficient crystallization of glucans may require additional factors not yet introduced into yeast.
source: Second, the efficient crystallization of glucans may require additional factors that we have not yet introduced into yeast.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation.

claim: Early Starvation1 (ESV1) is a non-catalytic starch-binding protein whose absence causes altered granule morphology and starch turnover in Arabidopsis.
source: An interesting candidate is Early Starvation1 (or ESV1), a non-catalytic starch-binding protein whose absence causes altered granule morphology and starch turnover in Arabidopsis (Feike et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: ESV1 was proposed to facilitate the correct alignment of glucans within the granule matrix.
source: ESV1 was proposed to facilitate the correct alignment of glucans within the granule matrix, which in turn could indirectly control the accessibility and thus degradation rate of glucans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed function.

claim: The precise action of ESV1 remains unclear.
source: However, its precise action remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a caveat.

claim: Soluble glucans that fail to crystallize efficiently may be rapidly removed by starch-degrading enzymes in plant cells.
source: Third, it is possible that soluble glucans that fail to crystallize efficiently are also synthesized in plant cells, but are rapidly removed by the starch-degrading enzymes described above.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation.

claim: In yeast, soluble glucans would accumulate because the degrading machinery is absent.
source: In yeast, such soluble glucans would accumulate as soluble glucans, since the degrading machinery is absent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a consequence of the yeast system design.

claim: The definition of insoluble and soluble glucans is based on fractionation by centrifugation at 6000 g for 5 min.
source: Finally, it is also important to note that our definition of insoluble and soluble glucans in this context is based on the fractionation by centrifugation at 6000 g for 5 min.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a methodological note.

claim: Insoluble glucans with a tiny particle size may remain in the supernatant after low-speed centrifugation.
source: Insoluble glucans with a tiny particle size may remain in the supernatant after such a low-speed centrifugation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a caveat about the fractionation method.

claim: Preliminary experiments suggest that half of the glucans in the soluble fraction from line 29 sediments upon extending the centrifugation to 20 min.
source: Indeed, preliminary experiments suggest that half of the glucans in the soluble fraction from line 29 sediments upon extending the centrifugation to 20 min (data not shown), indicating that at least part of it may actually be insoluble.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as preliminary data.
